t: What Flush Wire Cutters Are and Why PC Builders Need Them
title: What Flush Wire Cutters Are and Why PC Builders Need Them
description: Flush wire cutters — flush-cut snips — are small pliers whose jaws meet flat, cutting wire and zip-tie tails flush with the surface instead of leaving a pointed stub. For PC builders their main job is trimming zip-tie tails to a safe, finger-friendly edge, plus cutting component leads, wire, and small plastics. A 20-dollar pair is one of the highest-value tools on the bench.

demo.program:
jobs = ["zip-tie tails -> flush, finger-safe", "component leads", "hookup wire",
        "small plastic (standoffs, clips)", "beaded tie trimming"]
print("Flush cutter jobs:")
for j in jobs:
    print(f"  - {j}")
print("~$20: one of the highest-value tools on the bench.")

t: How Flush-Cut Jaws Differ From Diagonal Cutters
title: How Flush-Cut Jaws Differ From Diagonal Cutters
description: Diagonal cutters (dikes) have beveled jaws that leave a pointed pinch on the cut end — fine for wire, bad for tie tails you will touch. Flush cutters grind one jaw face flat so the cut lands flush against the surface. The trade-off: flush jaws are thinner and must never cut steel, springs, or hardened wire — that chips the edge. Right tool, right material, or the tool dies.

demo.program:
print("Diagonal cutters: beveled jaws -> pointed pinch (ok for wire, bad for tails).")
print("Flush cutters: flat jaw face -> flush cut (safe tails).")
print("RULE: flush jaws NEVER cut steel/springs/hardened wire (chips the edge).")

t: Key Models: Hakko CHP-170, Xuron 410, and What Makes Them Good
title: Key Models: Hakko CHP-170, Xuron 410, and What Makes Them Good
description: The Hakko CHP-170 is the benchmark budget flush cutter — about 5 dollars, cuts copper wire to 16 AWG, with comfortable grips. The Xuron 410 Micro-Shear steps up edge quality and ergonomics for daily use. What makes a good one: cleanly ground flush faces, jaws that meet with no gap, spring-loaded return, and grips that do not blister in an hour. Buy the Hakko to start; upgrade when you wear it out.

t: Cutting Capacity: What Flush Cutters Can and Cannot Cut
title: Cutting Capacity: What Flush Cutters Can and Cannot Cut
description: Standard 5-inch flush cutters handle soft copper wire up to 16 AWG, component leads, nylon zip ties, and small plastics. They must not cut steel wire, guitar strings, hardened pins, or live mains — the thin flush edge chips or folds. Micro flush cutters trade capacity for precision on tiny leads. When in doubt about the material, use the beater diagonal cutters, not the good flush pair.

demo.program:
can = ["copper wire to 16 AWG", "component leads", "nylon zip ties", "small plastics"]
cannot = ["steel wire", "springs", "hardened pins", "live mains"]
print("CAN cut:", ", ".join(can))
print("NEVER cut:", ", ".join(cannot), "(chips the thin flush edge)")
print("Doubt about material -> use beater dikes, not the good flush pair.")

t: Technique: The Perfect Flush Zip-Tie Tail Cut
title: Technique: The Perfect Flush Zip-Tie Tail Cut
description: Hold the tie head steady, lay the cutter's flat face directly against the head, and squeeze in one smooth motion — the tail shears flush with the head face. Cut straight across, not at an angle. Then run a fingertip over the cut: smooth means done, any scratch means re-cut closer. One smooth squeeze beats two nibbles, which leave steps in the edge.

demo.program:
print("1. flat face of cutter AGAINST the tie head")
print("2. one smooth squeeze (not nibbles)")
print("3. fingertip test: smooth = done, scratch = re-cut closer")
print("Angled cuts leave edges: cut straight across the head face.")

t: Use Case: Full-Case Tie Cleanup After a Build
title: Use Case: Full-Case Tie Cleanup After a Build
description: After strapping a build, every tie tail gets the flush treatment before the side panel closes: work methodically front to back, cut each tail at its head, finger-test as you go. A full tower can have 30 tails — ten minutes of cleanup. Skipping it guarantees bloody knuckles on the next upgrade; the cleanup is part of the build, not optional finishing.

print("Method: front to back, cut at head, finger-test each.")
print("Skipped cleanup = bloody knuckles next upgrade. It's part of the build.")

t: Use Case: Trimming Component Leads and Jumpers
title: Use Case: Trimming Component Leads and Jumpers
description: Through-hole component leads (on fan controllers, LED strips, custom PCBs) trim flush after soldering with the flat face against the board — no stubs to short against the case. Jumper wires cut to length with flush cutters get clean ends that seat fully in headers. The flush cut matters wherever a stub could touch something it should not.

demo.program:
print("Through-hole leads: flat face to board, trim after soldering (no short stubs).")
print("Jumper wires: flush ends seat fully in headers.")
print("Rule: wherever a stub could touch something wrong, cut flush.")

t: Ergonomics: Grips, Springs, and Hand Fatigue
title: Ergonomics: Grips, Springs, and Hand Fatigue
description: An hour of tie trimming punishes bad grips. Look for cushioned, slightly flared grips that do not pinch the palm, a return spring so your hand does not do the opening work, and a size matched to your hand — 5-inch cutters suit most, smaller hands may prefer 4-inch micro. If your forearm aches after a build, the tool is wrong, not you.

demo.program:
print("Good ergonomics: cushioned flared grips + return spring + right size.")
print("5-in: most hands. 4-in micro: smaller hands / precision work.")
print("Forearm ache after a build = wrong tool, not weak hands.")

t: Maintenance: Cleaning, Oiling, and Edge Care
title: Maintenance: Cleaning, Oiling, and Edge Care
description: Wipe jaws clean after cutting anything gummy (tape, adhesive), put one drop of light oil on the pivot yearly, and store closed or sheathed so the edges do not nick each other in the drawer. Never use the cutters as a pry bar or screwdriver — side loads spring the jaws and ruin the flush meeting. A cared-for pair lasts years; an abused pair lasts one steel wire.

demo.program:
print("After gummy cuts: wipe jaws. Yearly: one drop of oil on pivot.")
print("Store closed/sheathed: edges nick each other loose in drawers.")
print("NEVER pry or screwdrive with them (side loads spring the jaws).")
print("Cared for: years. One steel wire: dead.")

title: Sharpening and When to Replace
description: Flush cutters are rarely worth sharpening — the flat face geometry is hard to restore by hand, and a 5-dollar replacement beats an hour of filing. Replace when cuts need two squeezes, tails show steps, or the jaws have a visible gap or chip. Keep the worn pair as the beater for rough jobs (cutting old ties out, dirty plastics) and the new pair for finish work.

demo.program:
print("Sharpening: not worth it (flat-face geometry, $5 replacement wins).")
print("Replace when: two squeezes needed, stepped tails, visible gap/chip.")
print("Retire old pair to beater duty (rough cuts); new pair does finish work.")

t: Flush Cutters vs Diagonal Cutters vs Scissors
title: Flush Cutters vs Diagonal Cutters vs Scissors
description: Flush cutters: flush safe edges on ties and leads — the PC finish tool. Diagonal cutters: stronger, for heavier wire and rough cuts where the edge finish does not matter. Scissors/shears: for velcro straps, tape, and soft materials — never for tie tails (they crush more than cut). The bench wants all three; each has a job the others do badly.

t: Buying Guide: What to Check in the Store
title: Buying Guide: What to Check in the Store
description: Open and close them: the action should be smooth with a light spring return. Sight down the jaws: they must meet along the full edge with no gap and no overlap. Check the flush face is truly flat, not roughly ground. Grip them like you will use them for an hour. Under 10 dollars gets a good starter; over 30 buys pro ergonomics and edge life for daily use.

t: Advanced: Cutting in Tight Case Interiors
title: Advanced: Cutting in Tight Case Interiors
description: Tails buried behind cable trunks need the cutter's nose: slide the flat face along the tie to its head by feel, verify position with a fingertip, then squeeze. For tails against the motherboard tray, approach from the side the head faces. A headlamp is mandatory — you cannot cut what you cannot see. Patience beats force in tight quarters; a rushed cut nicks the cable it was bundling.

demo.program:
print("Buried tails: slide flat face along tie to head BY FEEL, verify by fingertip.")
print("Approach from the head's facing side. Headlamp mandatory.")
print("Patience > force: rushed cuts nick the bundled cable.")
